strengths: Elegant and coherent theoretical framework: the paper cleanly shows that the classical RL policy gradient is the leading (k=1) term of a Maclaurin expansion of the maximum-likelihood objective in pass@k events, giving a principled, compute-indexed family of objectives (Eq. 4-7) that provably interpolates between RL and exact ML.

The proposed estimator requires only a single-line change to standard REINFORCE/GRPO-style advantage computation (normalize by number of successes K rather than total samples N), and the paper provides clean, correct proofs (Theorems 1-2, Appendix B) establishing exact unbiasedness for the truncated objective at each finite rollout count.

The 'unifying weight-function view' (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) is a valuable conceptual contribution: it reframes RL, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML on a common axis and gives an intuitive explanation for why GRPO over-weights easy examples relative to ML, connecting to and extending recent theoretical work (Davis and Recht, 2025).

Very broad and carefully staged empirical validation: a controlled differentiable setting (ImageNet/ResNet-50) where exact ML is computable and MaxRL is shown to track it as compute increases; a large-scale synthetic maze task isolating data/compute scaling; a data-scarce GSM8K setting probing overfitting/pass@k collapse; and billion-parameter Qwen3 (1.7B/4B) training on real math benchmarks — a much wider battery of experiments than most concurrent work on this topic.

Consistent comparisons against multiple modern baselines beyond GRPO/RLOO (PKPO, Differential Smoothing, entropy-bonus GRPO, SELF), with MaxRL Pareto-dominating across settings, strengthening the significance claim.

Thorough related-work treatment, explicit and honest positioning relative to the two closest concurrent papers (Xiong et al. 2025b; Davis and Recht 2025), and an extensive appendix with reproducible experimental/hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea—computing gradients only from successful rollouts and discarding all-failure prompts—is conceptually close to existing rejection-sampling/RAFT/STaR-style filtering; the main novelty is the theoretical framing (unbiasedness for a specific truncated ML series) rather than a fundamentally new training mechanism, which somewhat tempers the originality claim.

When K=0 (no successes among N rollouts) the estimator contributes zero gradient, identical in spirit to REINFORCE's vanishing-gradient failure mode on very low pass-rate prompts; the paper does not thoroughly characterize how many rollouts are needed as p→0 to avoid this failure, despite this being precisely the regime MaxRL is designed to help with.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or variance/statistical-significance analysis are reported for any of the main results (ImageNet, maze, GSM8K, or Qwen3 training), which is a notable gap given the well-documented run-to-run noise in RL/LLM training and undermines confidence in some of the more marginal comparisons.

The headline '20x test-time scaling efficiency' claim is based on a maximum over several benchmark/model combinations under an idealized 'perfect verifier' assumption used only to filter samples at inference; this is somewhat cherry-picked relative to the range reported (2.3x-19.2x) and may overstate typical practical gains in settings without a perfect verifier.

All experiments use a fully on-policy setup with no importance-ratio clipping or off-policy updates, whereas most large-scale RLVR systems in practice use PPO/GRPO-style clipped, mildly off-policy updates; the paper explicitly defers this extension to future work, leaving open how MaxRL interacts with the off-policy machinery used in production training.

The variance behavior of the proposed control-variate estimator is only partially analyzed; no quantitative bias-variance or sample-complexity study is given for how estimator quality degrades as pass rate shrinks or rollout budget N is limited, which is central to the paper's compute-scaling narrative.

The largest-scale LLM experiments (Qwen3-1.7B/4B) use comparatively modest training budgets (16 rollouts/prompt, 1000 steps) relative to typical RLVR pipelines, leaving some uncertainty about how the benefits scale to production-level training compute and larger models.

strengths: The central theoretical contribution—expressing the maximum likelihood objective as a Maclaurin series in pass@k events, showing that standard RL optimizes only the leading (pass@1) term—is elegant, mathematically clean, and gives a unifying 'weight-function' lens (Section 5, Table 2) that nicely explains and reinterprets existing heuristics such as GRPO's 1/sqrt(p(1-p)) weighting and PKPO's pass@k optimization as special cases of a single spectrum.

Theorem 1 (success-conditioned expectation form of the ML gradient) and Theorem 2 (exact finite-sample estimator-objective equivalence for truncation order T=N) are proven cleanly and give a very simple, almost drop-in modification to standard policy-gradient estimators (normalize by number of successes K instead of total samples N), which is appealing for ease of adoption.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a single paper: a fully differentiable control setting (ImageNet/cross-entropy) that validates the theory in a setting where ground truth ML is computable, a controlled infinite-data maze environment, a data-scarce GSM8K fine-tuning setting, and full-scale LLM RLVR training on Qwen3-1.7B/4B with four to eight math benchmarks.

Many relevant and recent baselines are included (GRPO, RLOO, GRPO+entropy, PKPO, Differential Smoothing, SELF), and the paper reports consistent, sizable improvements in both pass@1 and pass@k/coverage metrics across settings, which is a meaningful empirical signal.

Good supplementary mechanistic analyses (gradient-norm-vs-pass-rate scatterplots, fraction of prompts with non-zero pass rate during training, entropy and response-length dynamics) that attempt to explain *why* the method behaves differently rather than only reporting final metrics.
Reproducibility details (architectures, hyperparameters, prompts, data generation procedures) are thoroughly documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The practical estimator sets the gradient to exactly zero whenever a prompt yields zero successes in a rollout batch (K=0), which is precisely the regime of hardest, rarest-success problems that the paper claims maximum-likelihood weighting is meant to rescue; for competition-math-level training (16 rollouts/prompt on Qwen3) many of the hardest prompts may frequently have K=0, so the degree to which MaxRL is actually closer to true ML gradients versus RL in the regimes that matter most is not rigorously characterized, only argued asymptotically 'in the infinite-compute limit.'

A key potential confound is not controlled for: Figures 6 and 8 show MaxRL produces substantially larger gradient norms than GRPO/RLOO on hard prompts, yet all methods are trained with the same nominal learning rate. Since larger gradient norms imply larger effective parameter updates, part of the reported performance gap could stem from an implicit larger effective step size for MaxRL rather than from the claimed higher-fidelity approximation to the ML objective; a learning-rate-matched (e.g., gradient-norm-normalized) comparison or a per-method LR sweep would be needed to rule this out.

The headline claim of 'up to 20x test-time scaling efficiency gains' is drawn from the single best-case benchmark/model combination in Figure 5/Figure 11, while other combinations show gains as low as ~1.6x-2.3x; reporting the maximum across many cherry-picked comparisons in the abstract somewhat overstates the typical/expected benefit.

Experiments on large-scale LLMs use relatively short training budgets (1000 RL steps) and low rollout counts (16) on models up to only 4B parameters; it remains unclear whether the benefits persist with longer training, larger models, or the rollout counts actually used in state-of-the-art RLVR pipelines (often 32-256+ rollouts), limiting confidence that the conclusions transfer to frontier-scale training.

The paper's own 'closely related works' discussion acknowledges substantial conceptual overlap with contemporaneous work (Xiong et al. 2025b; Davis and Recht 2025), both of which independently identify log-weighting of pass rate and the success-conditioned-distribution viewpoint; the marginal novelty here is primarily the explicit finite-sample estimator-objective equivalence and the empirical scaling study, which is a real but comparatively narrower contribution than the framing ('a fundamentally different objective for RL training') suggests.

The population-level weight-function analysis (Section 5) is a useful heuristic but is derived under idealized assumptions (expectation over models/population, ignoring SGD noise, non-convexity, and practical implementation details like clipping, KL terms, and off-policy correction that are dropped entirely in the experiments); it is not established how well this population-level picture predicts behavior in the actual non-convex, mini-batch optimization regime used in the experiments.

No experiments are provided in some of the domains explicitly highlighted as motivating examples in the introduction (code generation, navigation beyond the synthetic maze, program synthesis), so the claimed broad applicability to 'correctness-based' domains is only partially substantiated.

strengths: Clean theoretical contribution: the Maclaurin/pass@k decomposition of the ML gradient (Eq. 5) gives a principled, interpretable account of why RL underweights hard/low-pass-rate prompts; Theorem 1 (success-conditioned gradient) and Theorem 2 (exact estimator-objective equivalence) are rigorously proven.

The weight-function unification (Section 5) is a valuable conceptual contribution explaining GRPO's counter-intuitive behavior (upweighting easy prompts) within the same framework as RL/ML, corroborated by gradient-norm analyses (Fig. 6, Fig. 8).
Implementation is remarkably simple (single-line change to advantage calculation vs. RLOO-style baselines), aiding reproducibility and adoption.

Extensive, well-designed empirical validation across four very different regimes (exact-ML ImageNet control, infinite-data maze, data-scarce GSM8K, and billion-parameter LLM reasoning), with consistent gains including pass@k degradation mitigation and up to 20x inference-efficiency improvements.
Thorough comparison against multiple recent baselines (PKPO, Differential Smoothing, GRPO+entropy, SELF) beyond just RLOO/GRPO.

Honest, detailed related-work discussion distinguishing the contribution from concurrent closely related papers, and clear statement of limitations (binary reward only, no multi-turn/off-policy extension).
weaknesses: Core LLM reasoning experiments use relatively low rollout counts (16) and few RL steps (1000) compared to typical production RLVR runs; unclear if gains persist or saturate at larger scale/longer training.

Restriction to fully on-policy training (no importance sampling/clipping/PPO-style updates) leaves open whether MaxRL integrates well with off-policy or multi-epoch-per-batch settings common in practice.

Variance of the estimator when K is small (low pass-rate prompts, large truncation T) is only partially addressed via a control variate; no formal variance analysis across truncation levels is provided.
The practical algorithm's zero-gradient masking when K=0 could interact with effective batch size and curriculum effects in under-explored ways.
The weight-function analysis is population-level/asymptotic; finite-sample bias/variance tradeoffs of the practical algorithm are characterized only empirically, not theoretically.

strengths: Clean and elegant theoretical framework: the Maclaurin expansion of log(pass-rate) in terms of fail@k events cleanly shows that standard RL (REINFORCE-style policy gradient) is exactly the first-order truncation of the maximum-likelihood objective, unifying RL and ML under one lens.

The proposed estimator (average score function over successful rollouts only) is simple, requires only a one-line change to standard RL code, and is proven (Theorem 2) to be exactly unbiased for the T=N truncated MaxRL objective; the practical variant with baseline subtraction and K=0 dropping is also carefully analyzed (Theorem 5) for its resulting effective truncation order, showing rigor and honesty about the gap between theory and implementation.

Extremely thorough empirical validation across a wide range of settings and scales: differentiable ImageNet classification (where exact ML/cross-entropy can be directly compared), infinite-data maze navigation, data-scarce GSM8K with SmolLM2-360M, and large-scale LLM reasoning training with Qwen3-1.7B/4B on POLARIS-53K, consistently showing Pareto-dominance over GRPO/RLOO.

Extensive ablations and baseline comparisons beyond the main text (PKPO, ZPD, Power-function weighting, entropy bonuses, differential smoothing, majority voting, gradient-norm and gradient-variance analyses, SNR analysis, distribution-sharpening/pass@k degradation analysis) substantially strengthen confidence in the robustness of the reported gains.

The unifying weight-function view (Table 2, Figure 1) that expresses RL, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML gradients all as population-level pass-rate reweightings is a valuable conceptual contribution that clarifies why GRPO differs qualitatively from a log-likelihood-motivated objective (including the interesting observation that GRPO's weighting inverts for large p).

Good scholarship and honest positioning relative to closely related concurrent work (Xiong et al. 2025b, Davis and Recht 2025), with a clear articulation of what is different (finite-sample estimator-objective equivalence vs. adaptive sampling or asymptotic characterizations).
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, architecture descriptions, and code/asset release are provided.
weaknesses: The core practical estimator assigns exactly zero gradient whenever no correct rollout is sampled (K=0) for a given prompt, which is precisely the regime (very low pass rate, hard problems) where the paper's theoretical motivation says MaxRL should provide the largest correction over vanilla RL; this fundamental limitation is acknowledged but not resolved, and the method's benefits are therefore bottlenecked by the sampling budget in exactly the hardest cases.

The extension to non-binary/continuous rewards (Appendix M.4) is presented only as a brief, single small-scale (16M parameter, toy maze) proof-of-concept without a full theoretical treatment, despite non-binary rewards being common in many RL applications; the core theory is restricted to binary correctness rewards.

The largest-scale LLM experiments use models up to only 4B parameters trained for 1000 steps on ~50K prompts; while reasonable given likely compute constraints, this leaves open whether the reported up-to-20x test-time efficiency gains and Pareto-dominance persist at frontier model scales, longer training horizons, or with more sophisticated RL infrastructure (e.g., PPO-style clipping, off-policy correction) that the paper explicitly defers to future work.

Some claims are speculative and based on limited evidence, e.g., the suggestion in Appendix M.3 that MaxRL induces capabilities 'beyond the base model' rests on only 3 AIME problems and a small perplexity analysis, which is interesting but far from conclusive and could be over-read by readers skimming the appendix.

The paper is very long (main text plus ~60 pages of appendix), and several important pieces of evidence and nuance (e.g., the K=0/no-baseline truncation-order mismatch, the extensive baseline comparisons) are relegated to the appendix; while thorough, this makes it harder to assess the core claims purely from the main text without consulting extensive supplementary material.

strengths: Clean, rigorous theoretical framework: the Maclaurin expansion of log p(x) in terms of pass@k events (Eq. 4-5) elegantly shows that REINFORCE-style RL is the first-order truncation of the maximum-likelihood objective. The proofs of Theorem 1 (conditional-expectation form of the ML gradient) and Theorem 2 (estimator-objective equivalence) are correct and non-trivial, and the paper is honest about the fact that the practical algorithm (with zero-gradient fallback) is actually unbiased for order N-1, not N (Appendix D).

The 'unifying weight-function view' (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution: it cleanly explains why GRPO's implicit weighting w(p) ∝ 1/√p(1-p) inverts at high pass rates and over-weights easy prompts, giving a principled explanation for previously only empirically observed pass@k degradation.

Extremely thorough empirical validation across a wide range of regimes: a fully differentiable control setting (ImageNet, where exact cross-entropy ML is available for direct comparison), an infinite-data maze setting, a data-scarce GSM8K setting, and billion-parameter Qwen3 LLM training on math reasoning. This breadth, combined with consistent qualitative trends (less pass@k degradation, larger gradients on hard prompts, less distribution sharpening), strengthens the central claim.

Extensive appendix with ablations that most papers omit: gradient-variance analysis of the proposed baseline, inverse-SNR scaling with rollout count, non-zero-gradient-fraction analysis, perplexity analysis suggesting capability expansion beyond the base model, and comparisons against many recent alternative objectives (PKPO, ZPD, Power Function, Differential Smoothing, SELF, entropy bonuses) rather than only GRPO/RLOO.

The proposed change is practically trivial to implement (one-line change to the advantage calculation), which increases the likelihood of adoption and reproducibility, and code/assets are promised to be released.
weaknesses: The core limitation that the paper somewhat undersells: MaxRL still assigns exactly zero gradient to prompts with zero successful rollouts (K=0), identical to REINFORCE/GRPO/RLOO in this respect. This means MaxRL does not address the cold-start/exploration problem that is arguably the more fundamental bottleneck for very hard problems; it only reweights signal among prompts that already have non-trivial pass rates. The 'concentrates gradient on hard prompts' narrative is therefore somewhat overstated for the hardest, currently-unsolved prompts.

Conceptual novelty is incremental relative to closely-related concurrent work acknowledged in the paper itself (Xiong et al. 2025b; Davis and Recht 2025; Walder and Karkhanis 2025): the idea that expected-reward RL underweights low-pass-rate prompts and that a log/harmonic reweighting approximates likelihood is already present in this literature. The paper's distinguishing claim (fixed-rollout estimator with an exact order-N equivalence) is a solid but relatively narrow technical delta.

The headline '20x test-time scaling efficiency' claim is drawn from a favorable subset of benchmarks (BeyondAIME, Minerva at 19.2x) while other benchmarks show much smaller gains (2.3x-7.9x in main results, and as low as 1.4x-1.7x in appendix extensions), so the headline number risks giving an inflated impression of typical performance; a more conservative aggregate statistic would be more informative.

Comparisons are conducted in a stripped-down on-policy setting with KL penalty and entropy bonus both disabled for all methods, and without PPO-style clipping/importance-ratio effects, which deviates from how GRPO/RLOO are typically deployed in practice; this could affect the fairness or external validity of the comparisons against 'real-world' GRPO pipelines that commonly use these components.

Scale remains modest (up to 4B parameters, 1000 RL steps, 16-128 rollouts) and all reported reasoning gains rely on an idealized 'perfect verifier' setting for efficiency claims; it is unclear how results transfer to larger models, longer training budgets, or realistic (imperfect) verifiers/reward models.

The non-binary reward extension (Appendix M.4) is only validated on a single small toy maze task (16M parameter model), so the applicability of MaxRL to the broad class of continuous/shaped-reward RL problems common in robotics and other domains remains largely unsubstantiated despite being advertised as a natural extension.

strengths: Elegant and clear theoretical contribution: the Maclaurin expansion of the log-likelihood objective in terms of pass@k/fail@k events gives a principled, interpretable account of why standard expected-reward RL (REINFORCE/GRPO/RLOO) underweights hard, low-success prompts relative to maximum likelihood, and this is formalized rigorously with clean proofs (Theorems 1 and 2, with careful treatment of the practical estimator's effective truncation order in Appendix D).

The resulting weight-function unification (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 1) is a valuable conceptual contribution that cleanly situates REINFORCE, GRPO, MaxRL, and ML on a single spectrum and gives a principled reinterpretation of GRPO's heuristic standard-deviation normalization.

The proposed estimator requires only a one-line change to existing RL pipelines (average scores over successful rollouts rather than over all rollouts, normalized accordingly), which is both practically appealing and a plausible driver of adoption if results hold up.

Very extensive empirical validation across a wide range of scales and regimes: a fully differentiable ImageNet/cross-entropy sanity check, a large procedurally generated maze environment (infinite-data regime), GSM8K with a small LM across many epochs (data-scarce/overfitting regime), and large-scale Qwen3-1.7B/4B RLVR training on math reasoning, with consistent qualitative trends (less pass@k degradation, higher gradient norm on hard prompts, larger fraction of prompts with at least one success) that corroborate the theoretical story.

Thorough comparisons against a good set of relevant recent baselines beyond vanilla GRPO/RLOO (PKPO, ZPD, Power-function weighting, differential smoothing, entropy bonus), with MaxRL generally performing as well or better, including the counter-intuitive finding that directly optimizing pass@k (PKPO) underperforms MaxRL even at that specific k.

Substantial supporting analyses (gradient variance/SNR with and without the control variate, non-zero-gradient fraction over training, per-prompt pass-rate distribution sharpening, perplexity analysis suggestive of capability expansion, and a preliminary non-binary reward extension), reflecting a commendable level of empirical rigor and self-scrutiny.

Good transparency about reproducibility (detailed hyperparameters and task descriptions throughout the appendix, promised code/asset release) and an honest limitations/future-work discussion (binary reward assumption, zero-gradient on fully-failed prompts, off-policy/PPO-style extensions left open).
weaknesses: The zero-gradient-on-all-failure issue is a non-trivial limitation that cuts against the paper's central motivation (upweighting hard problems): for the hardest prompts in a budget-limited regime, MaxRL still contributes exactly zero gradient, identical in this respect to REINFORCE/GRPO, and the paper's mitigation (increasing N) is simply more compute rather than an algorithmic fix; this tension deserves more front-and-center discussion rather than being relegated to an appendix proof.

Several of the core demonstrations use quite small models (3M-parameter maze transformer, 360M SmolLM2, ResNet-50), and while the headline LLM reasoning results scale to 1.7B/4B parameters, it remains unclear how the reported gains (e.g., up to 20x test-time efficiency) extrapolate to current frontier-scale models or more realistic (imperfect) verifier settings, somewhat limiting the generality of the strongest quantitative claims.

The extension to non-binary/continuous rewards (Appendix M.4) is only a single small-scale proof-of-concept without theoretical grounding, so the practical scope of MaxRL beyond binary correctness rewards remains largely unexplored despite many real RL applications involving continuous or shaped rewards.

The "Pareto-dominates ... in all tested models and tasks" framing and the headline 20x efficiency figure are strong claims; although broadly supported by the experiments shown, they depend on a perfect-verifier assumption for test-time scaling efficiency and on specific evaluation protocols, and some readers may view the claims as somewhat optimistically phrased relative to the more nuanced per-benchmark results (e.g., Qwen3 results show MaxRL improving 7/8 pass@k settings, not uniformly all).

The exploratory capability-expansion analysis (Appendix M.3, perplexity/solved-problem overlap) is interesting but based on a very small number of problems (3 extra AIME problems solved), so claims about MaxRL inducing genuinely new capabilities beyond the base model should be read as suggestive rather than established.
